description: A team of 4 friends, looking for an opportunity to build something outside of our classroom context for the first time. We are all looking forward to becoming engineers or working in the medical field.
summary:
Martian Map is a route planner for astronauts on Mars, like Google Maps for an EVA. You pick a starting point, a date and the spacesuit or rover you will use, and the app shows how far you can safely go, with the trip back included. You choose your oxygen reserve margin, and it calculates the oxygen, water and food the trip needs, its duration, and whether you will be back before sunset.

Between point A and point B, it finds the safest route using real NASA orbital and rover data: slopes from HiRISE (1–2 m) and CTX (~20 m), weather from the Mars Climate Database checked against Perseverance and Curiosity readings, radiation dose and natural shelters, soil type, and geologic points of interest along the way. Because Mars has no GPS and no magnetic field for a compass, it also exports an offline map and a step-by-step route sheet.

This matters because one wrong turn on Mars can cost a crew its oxygen margin. Martian Map could help plan safe EVAs to unexplored regions and choose science targets along the way.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Martian Map is a safety-first GPS for Mars EVAs (extravehicular activities). The astronaut picks a start point and a destination on a map of Mars, chooses to go on foot (xEMU suit by default) or by rover, sets a date, a departure time and an oxygen safety margin. The app then computes the safest route there and back, and gives a full safety report: oxygen needed, water, food, duration, return time, radiation dose, natural shelters, weather alerts and points of interest along the way.

HOW IT WORKS

The app downloads real Mars data live, only for the area of the trip:

- Terrain and slopes: HiRISE elevation models (about 1-2 m) where they exist, otherwise CTX (about 20 m), otherwise the global MOLA map. HiRISE is automatically re-aligned on CTX so slopes are in the right place.

- Soft sand and dust: THEMIS night-time infrared (loose sand cools faster than rock at night).

- Weather: Mars Climate Database (ESA/LMD), corrected with real measurements from Curiosity (REMS) and Perseverance (MEDA) when the trip is close enough to a rover.

- Radiation: the surface dose rate measured by Curiosity's RAD instrument, adjusted for altitude and for how much of the sky is hidden by the terrain.

- Geology: the USGS geologic map of Mars, to find ice-rich units, basalt and faults.

- Martian time and Sun position: NASA's Mars24 algorithm.

A path-finding algorithm (A*) then searches for the route that costs the least effort while avoiding danger: every step costs more on steep or sandy ground, and slopes of 30 degrees or more are forbidden (25 degrees when morning frost is possible). The search is done first on the whole area, then refined at 2 m along the chosen corridor. The return trip is computed separately, because walking uphill and downhill do not cost the same oxygen.

BENEFITS

- Safety first: it tells the crew when a trip is not safe and why (slope, oxygen, duration, battery).

- Planning in minutes what would otherwise require several specialists and datasets.

- Backup navigation if electronics fail: a downloadable offline map, GPX/GeoJSON tracks and a dead-reckoning sheet (heading, distance, step count, Sun position).

- Robustness: if a data source is unavailable, the app automatically falls back to another one and shows it in a "Diagnostic" panel.

INTENDED IMPACT

Martian Map is designed as a planning tool for future crewed missions (Artemis and Mars), and could also be used today to plan rover traverses or to choose and compare exploration sites. It also makes real NASA data understandable for students and the public.

TOOLS USED

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (single-page web app), the Leaflet library for the map, geotiff.js to read elevation data, and a small Python server to relay data from NASA/USGS/ESA servers. The site is hosted on Render and the code is on GitHub. We used FigJam for research and brainstorming and Google Slides for the presentation. We also used an AI assistant (Claude) for research, data analysis, coding and writing, as declared in the "Use of Super Intelligence" section.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

We approached Mars exploration like a "Google Maps" for astronauts: instead of the fastest route, it finds the safest one. It combines datasets that are usually used separately (terrain, soil, climate, radiation, geology) into one simple answer: can we go, by which path, and what do we need to bring?

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Astronaut needs (oxygen, water, food, suit endurance, carried weight), terrain hazards (steep slopes, soft sand, rough ground), weather (temperature, wind, dust-storm season, morning frost), radiation (galactic cosmic rays, solar storms, shelters), navigation without GPS, and the reliability of every number: each value shows its source, and the app states its limits (model estimates, not flight-certified).
